title: Move Zeroes
directAnswer: Move all zeroes to the end in place while keeping the non-zero order. The naive answer copies non-zeros into a buffer then pads zeros; the canonical answer keeps a write pointer for the next non-zero slot and swaps each non-zero forward — one pass, O(1) space, minimal writes.

rules: `write` marks the slot for the **next non-zero**; everything before it is already packed.
On a non-zero, **swap** it into `nums[write]` and advance `write` — this preserves relative order.
Skip zeroes entirely; `write` stays put so the next non-zero overwrites the leftmost zero.
Swapping (not just assigning) carries the zero to the back, so **no explicit padding pass** is needed.
Order of the non-zeros must be **stable** — never reorder them.
When all elements are non-zero, every swap is `nums[i]` with itself — correct and harmless.
whenToUse: In-place partition: keep some elements up front, push the rest to the back
Relative order of the kept elements must be **preserved** (stable)
`O(1)` space with a single pass and minimal writes
Any 'move all X to one side' rearrangement
antiSignals: Order doesn't matter → two-pointer swap from both ends is fewer writes still
Multiple categories to partition (Dutch flag) → three pointers, not one
You must keep zero positions too → this destroys them
Linked list, not array → splice nodes instead of swapping slots
remember.takeaway: A single write pointer that only advances on a 'keep' element is the canonical stable in-place partition. Swapping the kept element forward simultaneously slides the unwanted element back, so one pass does the whole job. The same shape powers Remove Element and the partition step of quicksort.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can do a stable in-place partition with a single write pointer and minimal writes, instead of using an extra array or doing redundant write passes.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Breaking the relative order of non-zeros, doing two passes (overwrite then zero-fill) when one swap pass suffices, or writing every element even when most are already in place.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Note the write pointer is the boundary of the packed region, explain why swapping preserves order AND removes the zero-fill pass, and mention the all-non-zero case swaps each element with itself (harmless).

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums`, move all `0`'s to the **end** of it while maintaining the *relative order* of the non-zero elements.

**Note** that you must do this *in place* without making a copy of the array.
understanding: Compact the non-zero values toward the front in their original order, and let the zeroes collect at the tail. It's a stable partition with two classes — zero vs non-zero — done in place with no auxiliary array.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must the relative order of non-zero elements be preserved?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the constraint that rules out the simpler swap-from-both-ends partition and forces a stable, order-preserving write pointer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: In place, or can I allocate a new array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In place. A copy is explicitly disallowed, so the answer must use O(1) extra space.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are there negative numbers?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Only the value 0 is special; negatives are ordinary non-zero elements to keep.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I minimise writes?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It's a common follow-up. The swap-only-on-non-zero approach writes nothing for runs of zeros and skips redundant self-overwrites where possible.

examples.explanation: Non-zeros 1,3,12 keep their order at the front; the two zeros fall to the end.
A single zero stays put; nothing to move.
Six non-zeros packed in order, four zeros at the tail.

approaches.name: Copy Non-Zeros to a Buffer (Naive)
approaches.whenToMention: State it as the obvious baseline, then note it allocates O(n) space which the prompt forbids.
hints: Ignore the in-place rule for a moment: how would you produce [non-zeros..., zeros...] in a fresh array?
Scan nums, appending every non-zero to a new list. Then append enough zeros to reach length n.
Copy that list back into nums. It's correct but uses an O(n) buffer — exactly what the problem says not to do.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to collect non-zeros and one to copy back → O(n) time. The result list holds up to n elements → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Build the answer in a separate list — first all the non-zero values in their original order, then enough trailing zeros to refill the length — and copy it back into `nums`.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** The target shape is literally *"non-zeros, then zeros"*. The most direct way to produce that shape is to gather the non-zeros, count how many zeros are missing, and append them. There's no overwrite hazard because we write into fresh memory, so it's trivially correct and order-preserving.

**Why it's order-preserving for free.** Appending non-zeros during a left-to-right scan visits them in their original order, so the buffer holds them stably. The zeros are indistinguishable from each other, so 'maintaining their order' is vacuous — we just pad with the right count.

**Why it violates the spec.** The problem says *"do this in place without making a copy"*. This solution makes exactly that copy: an `O(n)` auxiliary list. Functionally fine, judged-correct on many platforms, but it sidesteps the skill the question is testing — rearranging within the original array.

**Why we still bring it up.** It pins down the goal shape and the stability requirement in the simplest possible terms. The optimal solution is really just this idea with the buffer eliminated: instead of writing non-zeros into a new list, write them into the front of `nums` itself with a write pointer, and let swaps carry the zeros to the back.
approaches.insight: The naive version makes the target shape obvious — non-zeros first, zeros after. The only flaw is the extra array; replacing it with an in-place write pointer over nums removes the O(n) space while keeping the exact same logic.

dryRun.intro: Collect non-zeros, then pad with zeros to length 5, then copy back.

code.python:
def moveZeroes(self, nums: list[int]) -> None:
    buf = [x for x in nums if x != 0]
    buf += [0] * (len(nums) - len(buf))
    nums[:] = buf

java.explanation: Append each non-zero in order; the rest of buf stays 0 by Java's default init.
Copy the rearranged buffer back — this is the O(n) copy the prompt forbids.

python.line: buf = [x for x in nums if x != 0]

pitfalls: Allocating a buffer violates the in-place requirement — baseline only.
Forgetting to pad zeros to the original length leaves nums too short (Python) or stale (Java).

approaches.name: Write Pointer with Swap (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'a write pointer for the next non-zero slot; swap each non-zero forward'.
hints: You don't need a second array — the front of nums can be the output region. What invariant lets you safely place non-zeros there as you scan?
Keep write = index of the next slot that should receive a non-zero. Scan with read; everything in nums[0..write-1] is the packed non-zero prefix.

When nums[read] is non-zero, swap it into nums[write] and increment write. The swap sends whatever was at write (a zero, once we've passed one) back to read's position. Zeros never advance write, so they pool at the end.
approaches.complexityReasoning: read makes one pass (O(n)); each step is O(1). Only two index variables are used → O(1) space. Swaps occur once per non-zero, so writes are minimal — runs of zeros cost nothing.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain a `write` index marking where the next non-zero belongs. Scan with `read`. Whenever `nums[read]` is non-zero, swap it into `nums[write]` and advance `write`. Zeros are passed over, so `write` lags behind `read` and the gap between them is exactly the zeros seen so far.

**The invariant.** At all times `nums[0..write-1]` holds the non-zero values encountered so far, in their original order, and `nums[write..read-1]` holds only zeros. `write <= read` always, so the slot we swap into has already been read — we never lose data. When the scan finishes, the non-zeros fill the front stably and every zero has been pushed past `write` to the tail. This is the same write-head-trails-read-head guarantee behind every stable in-place partition.

**Why swapping (not just assigning) is the elegant move.** A two-pass alternative overwrites `nums[write++] = nums[read]` for each non-zero, then loops again to zero out `nums[write..n-1]`. The swap fuses those passes into one: when `write` is behind `read`, the slot at `write` is guaranteed to hold a zero (every non-zero before `read` was already pulled forward), so swapping deposits the non-zero up front *and* carries that zero back to `read`'s position in a single operation. No separate zero-fill pass is needed.

**Why order is preserved.** We scan left to right and only ever move a non-zero forward into the lowest available slot. Two non-zeros `a` before `b` in the input are written in that same sequence — `a` claims a smaller `write` than `b` — so their relative order is intact. Stability falls out of always filling the front-most free slot.

**Why writes are minimal.** `write` advances only on non-zeros, so runs of zeros do zero work. And when `write == read` (no zeros seen yet), the swap is `nums[i]` with itself — a harmless no-op you can optionally guard with `if (write != read)` to avoid redundant writes. Compared to the unconditional two-pass overwrite, this touches each element at most once.
approaches.insight: One write pointer that advances only on 'keep' elements is the canonical stable partition. The swap does double duty — it places the non-zero and evicts a zero in the same step — which is why a single pass with no zero-fill suffices. Recognise this shape and Remove Element, Sort Colors, and quicksort's partition all become variations on it.

diagrams.title: Gap between write and read is the zero count
diagrams.caption: nums[0..write-1] are packed non-zeros; nums[write..read-1] are zeros awaiting eviction.

pitfalls: Doing two passes (overwrite then zero-fill) when one swap pass suffices.
Advancing write on zeros — breaks the packing and the ordering.
Assigning nums[write] = nums[read] without swapping, then forgetting to zero out the tail.
Reordering non-zeros (e.g. swapping from both ends) — violates the stability requirement.

commonMistakes: Breaking the relative order of the non-zero elements.
Using an O(n) buffer despite the explicit in-place requirement.
Two passes (overwrite then pad zeros) instead of a single swap pass.
Advancing the write pointer on zeros, scattering them through the array.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overwrite without restoring zeros
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Copying nums[write++] = nums[read] for non-zeros packs the front but leaves stale values in the tail. Without a second pass to zero-fill, the array is wrong.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Swapping from both ends breaks order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Partitioning by swapping a zero at the front with a non-zero at the back is fewer writes, but it scrambles the relative order of non-zeros, which this problem forbids.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Advancing write on zeros
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If write moves forward for zeros too, non-zeros land in wrong slots and zeros get interleaved instead of pooling at the end.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
write = 0
for read in range(len(nums)):
    nums[write], nums[read] = nums[read], nums[write]
    write += 1  # advances even for zeros

patternNote: Canonical stable in-place partition with a single write pointer. Recognise it whenever you must keep a subset of elements up front in order and push the rest to the back with O(1) space. Swapping fuses the pack and evict into one pass. Same shape as Remove Element, Sort Array By Parity, and quicksort's partition step.
